clinicalPearls: A rare, chronic, sterile pustular eruption of the distal fingers and toes, widely regarded as a localised variant of pustular psoriasis affecting the acral skin.
Characteristically begins on one or two digits, often after localised trauma, as recurrent crops of sterile pustules on an erythematous, glistening base that coalesce into lakes of pus.
Progressive nail-apparatus destruction is a hallmark: pustules under and around the nail plate cause onycholysis, nail dystrophy and eventual anonychia (permanent nail loss).
Advanced disease produces osteolysis of the distal phalanx with tapering, sclerodactyly-like atrophy and shortening of the digit tip.
Pustules are sterile on routine culture; secondary bacterial or candidal colonisation is common and can obscure the diagnosis, but the underlying process is not infective.
May remain confined to a single digit for years or generalise into von Zumbusch-type generalised pustular psoriasis, sometimes with fever and systemic upset.
IL-36 pathway dysregulation links it to other pustular psoriasis variants; a subset carry IL36RN (DITRA), CARD14 or AP1S3 mutations.
Notoriously refractory to therapy; retinoids and biologics targeting TNF, IL-17, IL-23 and the IL-36 receptor are used, with anti-IL-36 agents of particular mechanistic interest.
reference.pathophysiology: Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau is considered a distinct, acrally restricted form of pustular psoriasis in which innate immune dysregulation drives sterile neutrophilic pustulation of the distal digits and nail apparatus. Overactivity of the interleukin-36 axis is central: loss-of-function variants in IL36RN (encoding the IL-36 receptor antagonist), and in some patients CARD14 or AP1S3 variants, remove the normal brake on IL-36 signalling, amplifying keratinocyte-derived pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that recruit neutrophils into the epidermis. Histologically this manifests as spongiform pustules of Kogoj within a psoriasiform epidermis, mirroring other pustular psoriasis subtypes. The predilection for the fingertip and nail unit, often triggered by local trauma (a Koebner-type phenomenon), produces relentless subungual and periungual pustulation; sustained inflammation of the nail matrix and bed leads to onycholysis, nail-plate dystrophy and ultimately permanent anonychia, while chronic inflammation extending to the distal phalanx causes osteitis and osteolysis with atrophy and shortening of the affected digit.
additionalDifferentials: Palmoplantar pustulosis and generalised pustular psoriasis (spectrum overlap)
Chronic paronychia with secondary bacterial or candidal infection
Herpetic whitlow and other herpes simplex infection of the digit
Parakeratosis pustulosa and contact dermatitis of the fingertip
Acral pustular vasculitis or Sweet syndrome affecting the hands
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing spongiform pustules of Kogoj in a psoriasiform epidermis
Bacterial, fungal and viral swabs of pustules to exclude infection and secondary colonisation
Radiography of the affected digit to detect distal phalangeal osteolysis and bone atrophy
Genetic testing for IL36RN, CARD14 and AP1S3 variants in early-onset or refractory disease
Screening for features of psoriatic arthritis and other psoriasis phenotypes
Baseline bloods and infection screening prior to systemic retinoid or biologic therapy
redFlags: Progressive nail destruction with digital tapering and radiographic bone loss indicating irreversible osteolysis
Transition to generalised pustular psoriasis with fever, malaise and widespread pustulation
Signs of secondary sepsis from superinfected pustular skin
Rapidly spreading pustulation proximal to the original digit
reference.prognosis: The course is chronic, relapsing and characteristically treatment-resistant, and untreated disease frequently causes permanent nail loss and disabling atrophy of the fingertip. Prognosis has improved with targeted biologic therapy, though flares and progression to generalised pustular psoriasis remain possible.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing sterile pustules as bacterial or fungal infection and treating with repeated antimicrobials alone
Delaying systemic or biologic therapy until irreversible osteolysis and anonychia have developed
Overlooking triggering trauma and continued Koebnerisation of the affected digit
Failing to recognise progression to life-threatening generalised pustular psoriasis
Attributing nail changes to onychomycosis without biopsy or imaging
